opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think when people first hear "olfaction data set," they picture a big table: a molecule on one side, a handful of descriptor words on the other, like "vanilla," "smoky," "fruity." And that's genuinely useful. A lot of our early work was built on exactly that kind of data, where expert panelists smell a purified compound and pick from a lexicon of descriptors. But that's really just the front door.

One way I think about it is that smell is a sense, and a sense is a whole pipeline. You've got the physical world, which is molecules floating through the air. Then there's the biology, receptors in the nose binding those molecules. Then there's perception, what a person actually reports experiencing. And then there's behavior and context, what you do with that perception. Each of those layers can produce data, and each can constrain a model in a different way.

At the chemistry level, you'd want more than a molecular graph. Things like volatility, vapor pressure and concentration matter enormously, because the same molecule can smell completely different at different intensities. Some sulfur compounds are pleasant at trace levels and awful at high ones. And most real smells aren't single molecules. A coffee or a rose is hundreds of compounds, so mixture data is huge, and it's much harder to collect.

At the biological level there's receptor activation data. Humans have roughly 400 olfactory receptor types, and mapping which molecules activate which receptors, and how strongly, gives you a kind of intermediate representation that's closer to what the brain actually gets as input.

Then on the perceptual side, there's a lot beyond descriptor labels. You can collect similarity judgments, asking whether two things smell alike, which sidesteps the problem that people don't share a precise vocabulary for smell. You can collect intensity and pleasantness ratings. And you can capture variation across people, since genetics, culture and experience shape what we perceive. Some people literally can't smell certain compounds.

And beyond that, there's the stuff that's really exciting to me: natural, in-the-wild data. Which odors show up in which foods, products or environments, how things change over time as fruit ripens or food spoils, and even links to health, since disease can change the volatile profile a body gives off.

So my view is that the labeled-molecule data set is like ImageNet for smell, an important starting point, but the field gets interesting when you build data that covers mixtures, concentrations, biology, individual differences and real-world context. That's how you get from "predict the label for this molecule" to actually digitizing smell.

r001.rationale: The response mentions odors found in “foods, products or environments,” but does not clearly say that whole consumer products themselves can be smelled as dataset items.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the default framing is: here's a molecule, here's a label like "floral" or "musky," go learn the mapping. And that's a really useful starting point, it's what got us to a map of odor at all. But it's a pretty impoverished view of what smell actually is.

The first thing is that in the real world, almost nothing you smell is a single molecule. Coffee is hundreds of volatiles. A rose is hundreds. So a data set that only has pure compounds is missing the thing you actually care about, which is mixtures, and mixtures behave in genuinely nonlinear ways. Two things together can smell like neither one, or one can completely mask the other. So mixture data, with the actual concentrations, is a huge piece of it.

That points to the second thing, which is intensity and concentration. The same molecule at different concentrations can have different qualities, not just more or less of the same quality. Indole at low concentration smells floral, at high concentration it smells fecal. So a label without concentration is kind of a half-label.

Then there's who's smelling it. Human raters are noisy, and they're noisy in structured ways. People have genetic differences in their receptors, so some fraction of the population just can't smell certain compounds, and others find them overpowering. So instead of collapsing to one consensus label, you want the individual-level ratings, the panelist IDs, maybe even their genotypes, because the variance is signal, not just noise.

You can also go below the behavioral level. Receptor activation data is really valuable, which receptors fire in response to which molecules, and in animals you can go further and look at neural responses in the olfactory bulb or piriform cortex. That gives you something closer to the ground truth of how the system encodes odor, independent of the vocabulary people happen to have.

And the physical chemistry matters too. Volatility, how a compound partitions into mucus, how it binds in the nose. Those determine what actually reaches the receptors, and they're mostly left out when you just hand a model a structure graph.

Finally there's the sensor side. If you have an electronic nose or a GC-MS trace, that's a measurement of the stimulus itself, and you can pair that with perception. A lot of what we want in the long run is a model that goes from what's physically in the air to what someone experiences, and right now the data set we have is mostly a shortcut that skips the air part. So I'd say the richest olfactory data set is really a multimodal one, with chemistry, physiology, individual perception, and context all tied to the same stimulus.

r001.rationale: The response discusses mixtures such as coffee and roses, but does not state that whole consumer products can be included as items to be smelled.

astra-6.text:
I think of a molecular structure as one part of a much bigger observation. You have a molecule, or a mixture of molecules, but then you have to ask: At what concentration? In what context? Who’s smelling it, and what are you asking them to report?

You could collect descriptions—does it smell floral or woody?—but also intensity, pleasantness, or judgments of similarity. Sometimes asking whether two things smell alike gives you information that’s hard to capture with a vocabulary. And disagreement between people can be part of the data, rather than something you simply average away.

You can also think about measurements along the path from the chemical stimulus to perception: which receptors respond, what neural activity follows, and ultimately what behavior that smell produces. Those are different views of the same underlying process.

So an olfactory data set can be much more than a table mapping structures to words. It can capture the relationship between chemistry, the observer, and the conditions under which the observation happens.

r001.rationale: The response discusses molecules, mixtures, observers, and smelling conditions, but never states that whole consumer products can be dataset items.

sol-6.1.text:
I think molecular structures and odor labels are really just the starting point. You can ask, how intense is this smell? At what concentration can somebody detect it? How does it change as you increase the concentration? And then there’s the perceptual side: How similar are two smells? What words do people use to describe them? Do they find them pleasant or unpleasant?

You can also collect measurements at different levels of the system, from how a molecule activates a receptor to how a person experiences a mixture. And mixtures are especially important because most things we smell in the world aren’t single molecules. A cup of coffee is a collection of molecules, each present at a different concentration.

So the broader opportunity is to connect those kinds of observations. A molecular structure gives you one view, but a really useful olfactory data set starts to connect chemistry, biological responses, and human perception.

r001.rationale: The response discusses mixtures and uses a cup of coffee as an example, but it does not state that whole consumer products can be included as items to be smelled.
